overall_structure.value: Polycrystalline Fe-12%Al (real 12.0 at.%, 6.2 wt.-%, 60 ppm C) with a coarse grain structure (grain size of the order of 1 mm). Slow furnace cooling from 1100 °C produced fine thin platelike or rod-like precipitates (believed to be carbides) on the grain boundaries. Before deformation nearly no dislocations were present; after 5.5% compressive straining at 10^-4 s^-1 at room temperature the furnace-cooled alloy developed a dislocation cell structure.

source.reason: Microstructural description of the polycrystalline Fe-Al alloys (coarse grains, grain-boundary precipitates after slow furnace cooling) applies to the Fe-12%Al polycrystal; the TEM results (Fig. 6) describe the dislocation substructure of the furnace-cooled Fe-12%Al after 5.5% compressive straining.

unmapped_findings: Polycrystalline Fe-12%Al has a real composition of 12.0 at.% (6.2 wt.-%) Al with impurity contents C 50–60 wt.ppm, Si 60–90 wt.ppm and Cu <40 wt.ppm (Table 1, polycrystal 12; nominal 12).
The Fe-12%Al alloy (60 ppm C) showed only a weak effect of quenching, in contrast to the Fe-16%Al alloy (<20 ppm C) which showed a strong effect of quenching.
Before deformation only few straight dislocations were observed in the quenched Fe-12%Al, whereas nearly no dislocations were observed in the furnace-cooled alloy.

The carbides are believed to form from the presence of up to 80 ppm carbon; their amount was smaller for lower C contents, and only rare tiny precipitate particles were detected on grain boundaries of an alloy with only 20 ppm C after furnace cooling.
The compressed Fe-12%Al specimens were deformed by 5.5% compressive straining at 10^-4 s^-1 rate at room temperature for the TEM study (Fig. 6).
